maint1-by-much-slothfulness-the-building.reason: Ecclesiastes 10:18 and 10:10 are unpacked first; the plain why (small leaks grow because maintenance has no owner or calendar) and the answer (maintenance is a rate) arrive near the end.
maint1-by-much-slothfulness-the-building.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why do small leaks quietly become expensive repairs? Because decay keeps running whether you decide or not, and a small leak and a fallen ceiling are the same problem at two different times (Ecclesiastes 10:18). Nobody chooses the big bill. They decline the small one again and again. The answer is to work ahead, on a schedule.
maint1-by-much-slothfulness-the-building.example: ONE SEAL, THREE YEARS. Say a roof seal fails this spring. Fixed now, it is a repair. Left a year, it is the repair plus drywall. Left two years, it is the repair, drywall and framing, and in bad cases remediation, moving the tenant and a claim. Each year saying not yet was defensible. Together they bought the largest bill.
maint1-by-much-slothfulness-the-building.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why do small leaks quietly become expensive repairs? Because the roof is not waiting on your decision. Decay runs every day, and a system that fixes only what people complain about catches nothing until it is the expensive version. So give maintenance an owner, a calendar and a line in the budget, and treat it as a rate that runs as steadily as the decay. Sharpen the edge before you swing (Ecclesiastes 10:10). Wisdom directs in advance, at what has not broken yet.

teen.open: Why do little leaks turn into big repair bills? Because the damage keeps going every day you wait.
teen.close: So fix small things early and on a schedule, not just when someone complains. Sharpen the axe before you chop.

senior.open: The title asks why small leaks become costly. Ecclesiastes 10:18 shows decay and collapse are one problem separated only by time unattended.
senior.close: So the answer is to treat maintenance as a steady rate, with an owner, a calendar and a budget line. Wisdom aims in advance at what has not yet failed (Ecclesiastes 10:10).

maint2-called-by-name-and-filled-for-the.reason: Opens on Bezaleel as the first Spirit-filled person; what that means for today's tradespeople (honor them in pay, honest scope, asked judgment, thanks) is drawn out only in the second half.
maint2-called-by-name-and-filled-for-the.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Yahweh's choice of a builder say about the tradespeople who keep your properties standing? That their skill is a gift from Him, not a cost line. The first person Scripture reports as filled with His Spirit was a craftsman, Bezaleel, called by name for the work (Exodus 31:2-5). So the plumber and the roofer deserve the regard that gift calls for.
maint2-called-by-name-and-filled-for-the.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Yahweh's choice of a builder say about your tradespeople? That their workmanship sits in the same list as wisdom, understanding and knowledge, as a filling of His Spirit (Exodus 31:3). So honor it where it can be measured: pay promptly, write an honest scope, ask for the judgment of the man on the roof, and thank him in a form he would recognise by naming him, calling him back and referring him on. Yahweh named Bezaleel out loud before the work began. Learn the names of the people who keep your buildings standing.

teen.open: What does Yahweh think of people who build and fix things? The first person the Bible says He filled with His Spirit was a builder.
teen.close: So treat tradespeople with honor: pay them on time, be honest about the job, listen to them, and thank them by name.

senior.open: The title asks what Bezaleel's calling says about tradespeople today. He was called by name and filled with the Spirit for workmanship (Exodus 31:2-3), which places craft among Yahweh's gifts.
senior.close: So an owner honors that gift concretely: prompt pay, honest scope, the tradesman's judgment sought, and thanks given by name. Yahweh named His builder before the work began.

maint3-daubed-with-untempered-morter.reason: Ezekiel 13 is unpacked first; the plain answer (covering a stain destroys the gauge and grows the repair, so trace, fix and verify before any cosmetic work) arrives in the last two sections.
maint3-daubed-with-untempered-morter.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. The paint looks fine, but is the wall? Not if the paint went over a defect nobody fixed. Ezekiel calls that untempered mortar: a smooth face saying peace when there is no peace (Ezekiel 13:10). Covering a stain is a false report about the building, and it removes the one sign that told you water was getting in.
maint3-daubed-with-untempered-morter.example: THE BROWN CIRCLE. Say a ceiling shows a brown stain before a showing, and it is painted over the same afternoon. The room looks done. Behind the paint the drip continues, and now nobody can watch it spread. Months later the drywall softens and the joists are wet. A bounded repair became an unbounded one, and the gauge was gone.
maint3-daubed-with-untempered-morter.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The paint looks fine, but is the wall? You only know once the defect behind it has been traced to its source, corrected, and the correction verified. A stain is the building telling you the truth, and painting over it does not slow the water by a drop. It hides the growth until load arrives, the one moment the failure costs most (Ezekiel 13:11). So no cosmetic work goes over a defect until it is fixed and the trace is written down. Ask whether it is corrected, not whether it looks corrected.

teen.open: If the paint looks fine, is the wall fine? Not always. Paint can hide a leak that's still getting worse.
teen.close: So find the problem and fix it before you paint. Looking fixed and being fixed are not the same.

senior.open: The title asks whether a sound surface proves a sound wall. Ezekiel warns against daubing a weak wall and declaring peace (Ezekiel 13:10).
senior.close: So the wall is sound only when the defect is traced, corrected and verified before any finish goes on, with the trace written down for the next person.

maint4-for-they-dealt-faithfully.reason: Answers early with 2 Kings 12:15 (they dealt faithfully, so trust had been earned); then turns to the owner's side and ends on the owner's balance rather than landing why the crew was trusted.
maint4-for-they-dealt-faithfully.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why would a repair crew be trusted with cash before the books were checked? Because they had earned it. Scripture gives the reason in four words: they dealt faithfully (2 Kings 12:15). It is not a case against audits. It shows what demonstrated honesty, built over time, can be worth.
maint4-for-they-dealt-faithfully.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why would a repair crew be trusted with cash before the books were checked? Because they dealt faithfully, one honest transaction at a time: the quote is what is charged, the date is kept, overruns are raised before the money is spent, and mistakes are confessed by the one who made them. That trust is an asset, and it runs both ways. Pay on the stated term, write an honest scope, and treat his judgment as information you paid for. Then he will trust you too, and give you his Saturday when a pipe opens at four in the morning.

teen.open: Why would workers be trusted with money without being checked? Because they had proven they were honest.
teen.close: So trust is earned, one honest job at a time, on both sides. Keep your word, pay on time, and people will trust you back.

senior.open: The title asks why the crew was not made to account. The text says plainly: for they dealt faithfully (2 Kings 12:15). Trust had been earned over time.
senior.close: So trust is an earned asset on both sides of the job. The tradesman builds it with honest quotes and early disclosure, and the owner with prompt pay and honest scope.

maint5-stone-made-ready-before-it-was-br.reason: First lines read 1 Kings 6:7's 'so that': the site was quiet because the stone was finished at the quarry; the last line lands it: the temple was built at the quarry, the site is only where it was stacked.

maint6-wages-into-a-bag-with-holes.reason: Opens on Haggai's cieled houses; the plain answer (the 'saving' leaks out as call-outs, damage, vacancy, concessions, lost tenants, hours) only arrives mid-lesson; ends on an arithmetic instruction.
maint6-wages-into-a-bag-with-holes.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Where did the money go? When you put off the roof, the money you thought you saved did not stay saved. It left through channels nobody tracks: the emergency call-out, the ruined interiors, the empty unit, the rent concession, the good tenant who leaves, the hours lost to complaints. Haggai calls that a bag with holes (Haggai 1:6). Here is how he saw it before the bill arrived.
maint6-wages-into-a-bag-with-holes.example: ONE ROOF, SIX LEAKS. Say an owner declines a roof repair and books the saving. A year later the failure comes on a Saturday night, at the out-of-hours rate. The ceilings and floors below need drying and replacing. The unit sits empty while the work is done under pressure. The next tenant only signs with a rent concession. The good tenant upstairs does not renew. And the owner spends weeks of evenings on calls and complaints. None of those six lines sits next to the declined repair in the budget, so nobody ever sees the two totals together.
maint6-wages-into-a-bag-with-holes.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Where did the money go? Into the bag with holes. The deferred roof was never money kept; it was money that left later, at a worse rate, scattered across six lines that never sit beside the repair you declined. Haggai also shows it is a question of order: finish the structure before the panelling. Do the arithmetic once on one item you put off, and you will see where the money went, and stop sending it there.

teen.open: Where does the money go when you put off a repair? It does not stay saved. It leaks out later in bigger bills you never planned for.
teen.close: So where did the money go? Into what Haggai calls a bag with holes. Fix the important thing first, and the money stops leaking.

senior.open: The title asks where the money went. Haggai's answer is that a deferred repair is not a saving at all; it leaks away later through costs no one records beside the decision.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. The money went out through emergency rates, damage, vacancy and lost tenants, the bag with holes Haggai described. Tending the structure first is how you keep what you earn.

maint7-where-no-oxen-are-the-crib-is-cle.reason: Proverbs 14:4 is explained early, but the plain instruction (a low cost line is ambiguous, so always read cost beside production) arrives late; ends on talk versus labour, not on the paired reading.
maint7-where-no-oxen-are-the-crib-is-cle.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does the Word ask you to read maintenance costs alongside what they produce? Because a clean barn can simply mean there is no ox in it (Proverbs 14:4). The mess and the increase come from the same working animal. A low maintenance bill can mean real efficiency, or it can mean nothing was serviced at all, and the cost line alone cannot tell you which. Here is how to read it honestly.
maint7-where-no-oxen-are-the-crib-is-cle.example: TWO LOW BILLS. Say two buildings each show the same small maintenance spend for the year. In the first, the systems are sound, the service intervals were kept, and good trades fixed things once. In the second, nobody serviced anything, and the cost has simply moved into next year with damage attached. On the expense line they look identical. Put each beside what the building produced over the same year, and the difference starts to show.
maint7-where-no-oxen-are-the-crib-is-cle.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why read maintenance costs alongside what they produce? Because the ox that fouls the stall is the same ox that pulls the plough, and you cannot have the increase without the upkeep. A cost line read alone hides whether you were efficient or just neglectful. So set cost beside production on one page, for the building, the vehicle, the tools and the trades. Then act on it, because a repair that is only discussed is still failing.

teen.open: A clean barn can mean there is no ox working in it. Low repair costs can be good, or they can mean nothing is being cared for.
teen.close: So why look at costs and results together? Because the work that makes a mess is the same work that makes the increase. One number alone can fool you.

senior.open: Proverbs 14:4 observes that a clean crib may simply mean there are no oxen. A low maintenance bill is therefore an ambiguous signal, and the Word asks us to read it beside what the asset produced.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Cost and production come from the same source, and only read together do they tell the truth. Set them on one page, and then act rather than deliberate.

maint8-the-repairer-of-the-breach.reason: Opens on Isaiah 58:12's titles; the link the title promises (the name goes to those who keep the fast of bread for the hungry and the poor brought in) arrives mid-lesson; ends on a closing question.
maint8-the-repairer-of-the-breach.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gets called the repairer of the breach? In Isaiah 58, Yahweh gives that name to the people who keep the fast He chooses: bread dealt to the hungry and the poor brought into a house (Isaiah 58:7, 12). The name comes from that conduct, not from skill or portfolio size. That is the link: a building exists for the people under its roof. Here is how the chapter joins the two.
maint8-the-repairer-of-the-breach.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who gets called the repairer? The one who rebuilds old waste places, lays foundations that outlast him, and restores paths fit to live in, and does it because the building is for the people in it. Isaiah 58 refuses to separate the roof from the person under it. Strictly speaking there is no such thing as maintaining property; there is keeping a roof over a person. Do that, and Yahweh Himself gives you the name.

teen.open: Who does Yahweh call the repairer? Isaiah 58 gives that name to people who feed the hungry and bring the poor into a home.
teen.close: So who gets called the repairer? The person who fixes a roof because someone lives under it. Fixing buildings and caring for people are one job.

senior.open: The title asks who is called the repairer of the breach. Isaiah 58 gives that name not for technical skill but to those who keep the fast Yahweh chooses: bread for the hungry and shelter for the poor.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The repairer is the steward who keeps a roof over a person, building what will outlast him and restoring places fit to dwell in. That is work Yahweh named Himself.
